title.en: The World of Metals and Non-metals

text.en: A shopkeeper wraps food in aluminium foil, a worker coils a copper wire and a student writes with a graphite pencil. The materials have different jobs. Which property makes each one useful?

Many metals are shiny when their surfaces are clean. They often conduct heat and electricity well. Other properties, such as hardness, vary from metal to metal. Malleable means they can be beaten into thin sheets, like aluminium foil. Ductile means they can be drawn into wires, like copper. Many metal objects make a ringing sound when struck gently. The tendency to give a ringing sound is called sonority.
Many solid non-metals are brittle and conduct electricity poorly. Some non-metals, such as oxygen, are gases at room temperature. Oxygen and nitrogen are gaseous non-metals at room temperature. Mercury is a metal that is liquid near room temperature. We will study it from pictures. Graphite is a form of carbon that conducts electricity, an exception.
Many metals form oxides when they react with oxygen. Rusting is a specific change in iron or steel that requires oxygen and moisture. Some metals can release hydrogen when they react with certain acids. This extension depends on the particular metal and acid. Some non-metal oxides form acidic solutions in water. Carbon dioxide is one example.
Copper is used in wires, iron and its alloys in many tools, aluminium in foil and gold in some jewellery. These uses depend on a combination of properties.

Compare a piece of aluminium foil, a copper wire and a covered graphite sample in pictures. Each has a different use. Our first task is to name a property that helps with that use.
Look at a clean region of the metal surface and an older, dull region beside it. Surface changes can hide the shine, so a dull surface alone tells us little about the material beneath.
Follow a piece of aluminium in two factory sketches. It starts thick and ends as a broad, thin foil. Forming a sheet without the metal breaking shows malleability.
Now follow copper in a wire-making sketch. The end product is thin and long. The ability to form a wire is ductility.
Bending a piece may show flexibility, but it is a different observation. To support malleability, look for a piece flattened into a sheet, and to support ductility, look for a long wire.

board.text: Match the test to the property

text.en: Compare the sound of two objects in a teacher demonstration. One gives a ringing note and the other a short dull tap. The shapes are similar so the comparison is easier to interpret.
A metal spoon and a suitable wooden spoon can sit in the same warm-water demonstration. The teacher uses a thermometer to compare warming along the handles after the same time.
The metal handle generally warms faster because energy transfers through it more readily. Compare the readings after the same delay so the timing does not hide the difference.
Think of a low-voltage classroom circuit with a gap for a sample. A metal clip often lets the lamp light by joining the contacts in that gap.

board.text: Metal clip completes a conducting path

text.en: In a suitable test circuit, graphite can also allow current to pass. It is a form of carbon, so this result reminds us that conductivity alone cannot establish that a sample is a metal.

board.text: Graphite is a non-metal that conducts

text.en: Plastic and glass can be useful insulators. They are materials rather than examples of individual non-metal elements like oxygen and sulfur.
Compare pictures of an iron nail before and after time in damp air. A reddish brown layer forms on the second nail. That layer is rust, a new material formed from the iron.
Two matching nails begin in different settings. One has very dry air, and the other is in damp air. The difference in moisture helps us test what rusting needs.
A paint layer can help protect iron by keeping moisture and oxygen away. If the paint cracks, exposure can return in the unprotected spot.

The textbook shows a teacher demonstrating how magnesium reacts with oxygen to form a white powder called magnesium oxide. Study the before-and-after drawing to see that the powder is a different substance.

When a teacher checks the product with an indicator, a magnesium oxide and water mixture can show basic behaviour. Consider a different example: carbon dioxide dissolved in water can give an acidic result.

board.text: Magnesium oxide: can give a basic result

text.en: Materials vary. Iron can rust quickly in some conditions, while other metals can form thin surface layers that limit further reaction. Use evidence from the specific metal to describe its behaviour.
Non-metal elements matter in living things and in the environment. Oxygen is used by animals in respiration, and carbon is present in many substances that make up living organisms.

board.text: Carbon is present in living organisms

text.en: A tool maker needs a material that will hold its shape under ordinary use. A cable maker needs a conducting core that can form a long wire and a cover that insulates it.

board.text: Tools and wires need different properties

text.en: A dark sample makes a classroom lamp glow. How many properties have you checked so far? Explain why one observation cannot tell you whether it was graphite or a metal sample.

problem.en: Why are electrical wires made of copper?

text.en: Copper conducts electricity well.
It is also ductile and can be drawn into wires.

prompt.en: Explain how you would test if a material is a metal.

requiredIdeas.en: Compare several properties such as lustre, ability to form sheets and conductivity.

commonMisconceptions.en: One property is enough to classify every material.

points.en: Many metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile and good conductors.
Non-metals vary. Graphite is an example that conducts electricity.
Iron can rust when exposed to oxygen and moisture.
